blocks.content: The story starts with a decision you didn't realise you were making.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275485587-719848693.png
blocks.alt: An unversioned API change breaks every integrated client at once, months after launch

blocks.content: You launch your API. Developers integrate. Mobile apps go live. Enterprise customers build workflows on top of your endpoints. Months pass. Now you need to change something. A field needs a new type. A response needs restructuring. A behaviour needs to change to fix a fundamental design mistake.

You can't just change it. The moment you do, every client that depends on the current behaviour breaks silently or loudly. The mobile app that hasn't been updated in six months throws a null pointer exception. The enterprise integration fails at 3 AM during a batch job. The developer who built a weekend project six months ago gets angry emails from their users.
This is the API versioning problem. Not "how do I build versions" but "how do I evolve a shared contract without breaking the people who already depend on it."
Every strategy is a different answer to the same tension: you need to change, but others need stability.
1. Why versioning is necessary
An API is a contract. When you publish it, you're making a promise: "send me this, I'll return that." Clients build on that promise. The moment you break it, you break trust.

But products evolve. Requirements change. Design mistakes get discovered. What seemed correct at launch turns out to be wrong at scale. Without versioning, you have two terrible options: freeze the API forever (accumulate technical debt, never improve), or change it freely (break all existing clients).
Versioning is the mechanism that lets you say: "version 1 of the contract stays exactly as promised. Version 2 is a new, improved contract. Clients can migrate when they're ready."

The hard part: every versioning strategy creates maintenance burden. You're now running two APIs. Two sets of business logic. Two sets of documentation. Two sets of tests. The longer you support old versions, the heavier that burden becomes. Good versioning strategy is about minimising that burden while maximising stability for clients.

blocks.content: Strategy 1: URI versioning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275487564-45722487.png
blocks.alt: URI versioning puts the version number directly and visibly in the URL

blocks.content: The most visible, most common, most debated approach. Put the version number directly in the URL.

GET /v1/users/123
GET /v2/users/123
GET /api/v1/orders
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
blocks.text: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">

blocks.content: 1. URL Versioning
In URL versioning, the API version is included directly in the URL, such as /v1/users/123 or /v2/users/123. This makes it clear which API version the client is using.
2. What Works Well

The version is visible in the URL, making it easy for developers to understand and debug. CDNs automatically cache different versions separately because each version has a different URL. Routing is also simple, as gateways and proxies can forward requests based on the URL without checking headers.
URLs are easy to bookmark, share, document, and test. Different API versions can even be deployed on separate servers, making migrations much easier.
3. What Are the Limitations?
Whenever a new API version is released, clients must update their URLs from /v1 to /v2. If an application has many API endpoints, updating all URLs can take time.

From a REST perspective, some developers consider URL versioning less ideal because the resource remains the same, while only its representation changes. Ideally, the resource URL should stay constant.
4. Where Is It Used?
URL versioning is the most common approach for public APIs because it is simple, easy to understand, and works well with caching and API gateways.
Examples: Stripe, GitHub, Twitter (X), and many other public APIs.
Strategy 2: Header versioning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275489293-625816593.png
blocks.alt: Header versioning keeps the resource URL clean by moving the version into a request header

blocks.content: The version lives in the request header, not the URL. The resource URL stays clean.

GET /users/123
Accept-Version: v2

GET /users/123
X-API-Version: 2024-01-15
1. Header Versioning
In header versioning, the API version is sent in an HTTP header instead of the URL. For example, the request URL remains /users/123, while the version is passed using a header like X-API-Version: 2.
2. What Works Well

The URL never changes, so clients don't need to update URLs when a new API version is released. This follows REST principles because the URL identifies the resource, while the header specifies which version of the response the client wants. It also allows versioning logic to be managed centrally.
3. What Are the Limitations?
Since the version is hidden in the request header, it is not obvious which version is being used. This makes debugging, testing, and sharing URLs more difficult.

It is also less cache-friendly because CDNs cache based on the URL, not request headers, unless additional cache configuration is added. If a client forgets to send the version header, the server must decide which version to use, which can lead to unexpected behavior.
4. Where Is It Used?
Header versioning is commonly used for internal APIs, where clients are controlled and headers are easy to manage.
Examples: AWS services and Microsoft Azure APIs.
Strategy 3: Content negotiation (Accept header)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275490854-733338721.png
blocks.alt: Content negotiation encodes the version inside the Accept media type, the most REST-pure approach

blocks.content: The most REST-pure approach. Use the HTTP Accept header to specify the version as part of the media type.

GET /users/123
Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json

GET /users/123
Accept: application/json; version=2

GET /users/123
Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json

GET /users/123
Accept: application/json; version=2

GET /users/123

GET /users/123

codes.java:
GET /users/123
Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json

GET /users/123
Accept: application/json; version=2

blocks.content: 1. Media Type (Accept Header) Versioning

In media type versioning, the API version is specified in the Accept header instead of the URL. The URL stays the same, while the client requests a specific version using a media type such as application/vnd.myapi.v2+json.
2. What Works Well

This approach follows the original HTTP and REST design. The URL always identifies the same resource, while the Accept header decides which version of the response should be returned. This cleanly separates the resource from its representation.
3. What Are the Limitations?

The Accept header is long and difficult to remember, making it harder to write, test, and debug. It also has the same caching issues as header versioning because CDNs need extra configuration to cache different versions correctly. As a result, developer experience is not as good as URL versioning.
4. Where Is It Used?
Media type versioning is mainly used in APIs that closely follow REST principles. It is less common in practice because of its complexity.
Examples: GitHub (supports it along with URL versioning) and some enterprise APIs.
Strategy 4: Query parameter versioning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275492559-678905334.png
blocks.alt: Query parameter versioning is simple to try but easy for a client to forget to set

blocks.content: The version is a query parameter.

GET /users/123?version=2
GET /users/123?api_version=2024-01-15
GET /api/users/123?v=2
1. Query Parameter Versioning
In query parameter versioning, the API version is passed as a query parameter, such as /users/123?version=2. The URL stays the same, but the version is specified in the query string.
2. What Works Well

This approach is very simple to implement and can be added to existing APIs without changing the URL structure. It is easy to test in a browser and allows clients to switch versions by changing only the query parameter.
3. What Are the Limitations?

Using query parameters for API versions is generally not considered a REST best practice because query parameters are meant for filtering or searching, not versioning. URLs also become less clean, especially when multiple query parameters are used. Although it can be cached, some CDNs may ignore or remove query parameters, causing caching issues.
4. Where Is It Used?
Query parameter versioning is mainly used in simple or internal APIs where ease of implementation is more important than strict REST design.
Examples: Google Maps API and some internal APIs.
Strategy 5: Date-based versioning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027810-313587273.png
blocks.alt: Date-based versioning uses the date a contract was frozen as the version identifier itself

blocks.content: Instead of incrementing version numbers, use a date as the version identifier.

GET /users/123
Stripe-Version: 2024-01-15

# or in URI
GET /2024-01-15/users/123
blocks.code:
GET /users/123
Stripe-Version: 2024-01-15

# or in URI
GET /2024-01-15/users/123

# or in URI
GET /2024-01-15/users/123
codes.python:

Stripe-Version: 2024-01-15

# or in URI
GET /2024-01-15/users/123
codes.java:
GET /users/123
Stripe-Version: 2024-01-15

# or in URI
GET /2024-01-15/users/123

blocks.content: 1. Date-Based Versioning

In date-based versioning, each API version is identified by a release date instead of numbers like v1 or v2. Every API key is linked to a specific date, and the server returns the behavior that existed on that date. Developers upgrade by choosing a newer date when they are ready.
2. What Works Well

This approach allows developers to upgrade gradually instead of moving to a completely new version. Existing clients continue using their current behavior, while new clients automatically get the latest API version. It also makes API evolution smoother because changes are introduced over time rather than in large version releases.
3. What Are the Limitations?

The server must maintain multiple versions of the same behavior internally, which increases development, testing, and maintenance effort. Supporting very old versions also becomes difficult, and eventually older date-based versions need to be retired.
4. Where Is It Used?
Date-based versioning is commonly used by large public APIs that want to introduce changes gradually without breaking existing integrations.
Examples: Stripe and Adyen.
2. The deprecation lifecycle

Introducing a new version is the easy part. Retiring an old one is where most teams fail. A version that was supposed to live for 6 months ends up alive for 4 years because no one ever forced clients to migrate.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027810-481236299.png
blocks.alt: A version moves through active, deprecated, sunset, and removed stages before it actually disappears

blocks.content: Active: The API version is fully supported, receives updates, and is recommended for all clients.
Deprecated: The API still works, but it is marked for removal. Every response includes deprecation headers to notify clients that they should migrate to a newer version.
Example headers:

Deprecation: true
Sunset: Sat, 01 Jan 2025 00:00:00 GMT
Link: https://docs.api.com/migration/v1-to-v2
blocks.code:
Deprecation: true
Sunset: Sat, 01 Jan 2025 00:00:00 GMT
Link: https://docs.api.com/migration/v1-to-v2

codes.javascript:
Deprecation: true
Sunset: Sat, 01 Jan 2025 00:00:00 GMT
Link: https://docs.api.com/migration/v1-to-v2
codes.python:
Deprecation: true
Sunset: Sat, 01 Jan 2025 00:00:00 GMT
Link: https://docs.api.com/migration/v1-to-v2
codes.java:
Deprecation: true
Sunset: Sat, 01 Jan 2025 00:00:00 GMT
Link: https://docs.api.com/migration/v1-to-v2

blocks.content: Sunset Period: The retirement date is announced in advance. During this period, some requests may intentionally return errors to encourage clients to migrate before the API is completely removed.
Retired: The old API version is permanently removed. Any request to that version returns HTTP 410 Gone, indicating the API is no longer available.
Best Practices
Always inform clients before removing an API version by sending deprecation and sunset headers in every response.
Track which API version each client is using through logs and dashboards. Once almost all traffic has moved to the new version, the old version can be safely retired.
A gradual deprecation process gives clients enough time to migrate and avoids breaking existing applications.
3. Backward compatibility
The best versioning strategy is needing it as little as possible. Many API changes can be made without breaking existing clients if you understand what "breaking" means.
Non-breaking changes safe to make without a version bump:

["Adding a new endpoint","Adding new optional fields to a response","Adding new optional query parameters","Making a previously required field optional","Adding new enum values (with caution clients must handle unknown values)","Expanding a string field's maximum length","Adding new error codes to responses a client already ignores"]
items: Adding new optional fields to a response
Making a previously required field optional
Adding new enum values (with caution clients must handle unknown values)
Expanding a string field's maximum length
Adding new error codes to responses a client already ignores

blocks.content: Breaking changes: require a new version:

["Removing a field from a response","Renaming a field","Changing a field's type (string → integer)","Making an optional field required","Changing the semantics of an existing field","Removing an endpoint","Changing authentication mechanism","Changing pagination behaviour"]
items: Removing a field from a response
Changing the semantics of an existing field

blocks.content: The goal:accumulate many non-breaking changes and ship them freely. Reserve version bumps for genuinely breaking changes. If you can redesign a change from breaking to non-breaking (by adding a new field rather than renaming an old one, for example), do it. Every avoided version bump is months of maintenance saved.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 4. Implementation patterns
Build API versioning so only the response changes, while the core business logic remains the same.
1. The adapter / transformer pattern
blocks.text: 1. The adapter / transformer pattern

blocks.content: Don't duplicate business logic for each version. Maintain one internal data model and one set of business logic. Add a transformation layer that converts from internal to each external version.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275498075-409097513.png
blocks.alt: One internal model and one set of business logic, with a thin adapter translating to each external version

blocks.content: This pattern means: when you release v3, you write a new output adapter (v3 transformer). All existing business logic stays unchanged. When v1 is retired, you delete the v1 adapter. The business logic never changes.

The trap to avoid: duplicating business logic per version. If you copy-paste your GetUser handler three times for three versions and then need to fix a bug, you fix it in three places. Or forget one. The adapter pattern ensures you fix bugs once.
2. API gateway routing
At the infrastructure level, version routing can be handled entirely at the gateway before your application code sees the request.

# Kong / nginx routing example

routes:
  - name: users-v1
    paths: ["/v1/users"]
    service: user-service-v1
    
  - name: users-v2
    paths: ["/v2/users"]
    service: user-service-v2  # could be same service, different config

  # Header-based routing
  - name: users-versioned
    paths: ["/users"]
    headers:
      X-API-Version: ["2"]
    service: user-service-v2

blocks.content: For small changes between versions, you can run one service with internal branching. For large changes (microservices split, database schema changes), running separate service instances per version is cleaner you can deploy, scale, and retire them independently.
5. The strategy comparison
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275499735-403638771.png
blocks.alt: Each versioning strategy trades visibility, cleanliness, and REST-purity differently

blocks.content: 6. The Real-World Recommendation
Choose the versioning strategy based on who is consuming your API.

["Public APIs: For public APIs used by external developers, URL versioning is the best choice. It is simple, easy to debug, cache-friendly, and widely used by major companies.
","Internal Microservices: For communication between internal services, Header Versioning or Date-Based Versioning works well. URLs remain clean, and since you control all the services, version upgrades are easier to manage.
","Large Developer Platforms: For platforms with many external developers, Date-Based Versioning provides the best developer experience. Developers can upgrade when they are ready instead of moving to a completely new API version.
","What to Avoid: Avoid Accept Header Versioning unless you specifically need strict REST compliance. Also avoid Query Parameter Versioning for most APIs, as it is less clean and generally considered a weaker design choice.
"]
items: Public APIs: For public APIs used by external developers, URL versioning is the best choice. It is simple, easy to debug, cache-friendly, and widely used by major companies.

Internal Microservices: For communication between internal services, Header Versioning or Date-Based Versioning works well. URLs remain clean, and since you control all the services, version upgrades are easier to manage.

Large Developer Platforms: For platforms with many external developers, Date-Based Versioning provides the best developer experience. Developers can upgrade when they are ready instead of moving to a completely new API version.

What to Avoid: Avoid Accept Header Versioning unless you specifically need strict REST compliance. Also avoid Query Parameter Versioning for most APIs, as it is less clean and generally considered a weaker design choice.

blocks.content: 7. HLD Interview. ( How to Talk About API Versioning )
blocks.text: 7. HLD Interview. ( How to Talk About API Versioning )

blocks.content: When asked about API versioning, first explain the goal. API versioning allows us to add new features and improve the API without breaking existing clients.

For a public API, I'd choose URI versioning (/v1, /v2) because it's simple, explicit, cache-friendly, and easy to debug. Developers immediately know which version they're using, and API gateways and CDNs can route and cache requests easily.

Not every change requires a new version. Adding optional fields or new endpoints is backward compatible, so the same version can be used. A new version is only needed for breaking changes, such as removing fields, renaming fields, or changing data types.

To avoid maintaining duplicate code, I'd use the Adapter Pattern. The business logic remains the same, while version-specific adapters transform requests and responses for each API version. When an old version is retired, only its adapter is removed.

I'd also define a clear version lifecycle. When a new version is released, the old version is marked as deprecated, clients receive deprecation and sunset notices, and after sufficient time the old version is retired. Monitoring helps identify which clients are still using older versions.

Finally, the best versioning strategy is to avoid unnecessary versions. Design APIs to be backward compatible whenever possible by preferring additive changes over breaking changes. This reduces maintenance for both the API team and its users.
